dervis-irab:1-19.t:
* Vocabulary:
(العلق): blood. It is a collective generic noun, and the commentators have applied the plural to it, either loosely, or as a linguistic plural. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Al-ʿalaq is semen, which moves from stage to stage and becomes thick, congealed blood; then it moves to another stage and becomes flesh, which is the muḍgha." The wording of al-Qāmūs: "Al-ʿalaq, with vowelled middle letter, is blood in general, or very red blood, or thick blood, or congealed blood, a piece of it being with the tāʾ marbūṭa; and everything that clings; and the mud that clings to the hand; and the quarrel and love that are inseparable; Dhū ʿAlaq is a mountain of the Banū Asad, who had a battle day there against Rabīʿa ibn Mālik; and a small creature in water that sucks blood," to the end of what is given under this lengthy root.
(لَنَسْفَعاً): al-safʿ is seizing and grasping a thing and pulling it hard. In al-Mukhtār: "Safaʿa bi-nāṣiyatihi means he seized it; and from it comes His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿لَنَسْفَعاً بِالنَّاصِيَةِ﴾. Safaʿathu al-nār and al-samūm: when it scorched him lightly, changing the colour of the skin; their pattern is qaṭaʿa."
(الزَّبانِيَةَ): the stern, harsh angels. The singular is zabaniya, with kasra on the first letter, sukūn on the second, kasra on the third and a light yāʾ, from al-zabn, which is pushing; or zabanī by attribution, its original being zabānī with a doubled letter, in which the tāʾ is a replacement for the wāw. In al-Mukhtār: "One of the zabāniya is zabān or zābān. Al-Akhfash said: their singular is zabānī. Some said zābī, and some said zabniya like ʿifrīya." In al-Qāmūs: "Al-zabniya, like hibriya, is the rebellious among jinn and humans, the harsh one, and the policeman; the plural is zabāniya, or its singular is zabbanī."

* I'rab:
(اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ، خَلَقَ الْإِنْسانَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ): (اقْرَأْ) is an imperative verb indeclinable on sukūn, its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you". (بِاسْمِ) is attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial) from the pronoun of the agent, i.e. "beginning". Ibn Khālawayh parsed the bāʾ as redundant, following Abū ʿUbayda in that. He said: the bāʾ is redundant and the meaning is "recite the name of your Lord", as He said ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ﴾, and he cited: "Black-eyed, they do not recite from the sūras" (lā yaqraʾna bi-l-suwar), the meaning, on the bāʾ's being redundant, being "they do not recite the sūras". The discussion of the redundant bāʾ was given before. The wording of Abū al-Baqāʾ: "His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ﴾: it is said that the bāʾ is redundant, like the poet's 'lā yaqraʾna bi-l-suwar'; and it is said that it entered to alert to beginning with His name in everything, as the Exalted said ﴿بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾. On this view it may be a ḥāl, i.e. 'beginning with the name of your Lord'." (الَّذِي) is an adjective of (الرَّبِّ), in the position of a genitive, and the clause (خَلَقَ) has no grammatical position because it is the ṣila of (الَّذِي), the pronoun in it referring to (الَّذِي). (خَلَقَ الْإِنْسانَ) is a badal (substitute) for it, and it may be verbal emphasis (tawkīd lafẓī), in which case the ṣila alone has been emphasised. (الْإِنْسانَ) is the direct object, and (مِنْ عَلَقٍ) is attached to (خَلَقَ).
(اقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ الْأَكْرَمُ الَّذِي عَلَّمَ بِالْقَلَمِ): (اقْرَأْ) is an imperative verb, an emphasis of the first (اقْرَأْ). The wāw is resumptive, and it may be a wāw of ḥāl. (رَبُّكَ) is the mubtadaʾ and (الْأَكْرَمُ) is its khabar; this is what we have seen. Ibn Khālawayh parsed it as an adjective, in which case the clause (عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسانَ) is the khabar, but the first is preferable. (الَّذِي) is a second khabar; Ibn Khālawayh parsed it as a second adjective, but we do not hold this opinion. The clause (عَلَّمَ) is a ṣila, and the agent of (عَلَّمَ) is a latent pronoun referring to Allah, and its two objects are omitted, i.e. "He taught man writing by the pen". (بِالْقَلَمِ) is attached to (عَلَّمَ), and in fact it is attached to writing. [Translator's note: the Arabic printed here reads «الحظ» (fortune); «الخط» (writing) is evidently meant, and the translation follows the evident sense.]
(عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسانَ ما لَمْ يَعْلَمْ): The clause (عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسانَ) is an emphasis of the first (عَلَّمَ), or a badal, or a khabar, as mentioned before. (الْإِنْسانَ) is the first direct object; (ما) is a relative noun, the second direct object; the clause (لَمْ يَعْلَمْ) is the ṣila of (ما), and the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e. "he did not know it".
(كَلَّا إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ لَيَطْغى): (كَلَّا) is a rebuke and reproof to whoever disbelieves in Allah's favour upon him through his rebellion. (إِنَّ) with its noun, the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa), and the clause (يَطْغى) is the khabar of (إِنَّ). I do not know why the parsers fled from rebuke, which is clearer than all they implied, and to which al-Zamakhsharī went. As for al-Jalāl, he followed al-Kisāʾī and made it have the sense of ḥaqqan (truly). Al-Karkhī said: "His saying, that is, al-Jalāl's, ḥaqqan, is the view of al-Kisāʾī and those who followed him, because there is nothing before or after it that kallā could be a rejection of, as they said 'kallā wa-l-qamar', whose meaning, they said, is 'yes, by the moon'. The view of Abū Ḥayyān is that it has the sense of alā, the opening particle, and Ibn Hishām endorsed it because of the kasra of the hamza of inna after it, that is, because it is the likely place of a clause, as after a particle of alerting, such as ﴿أَلا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ الْمُفْسِدُونَ﴾; and had it been in the sense of ḥaqqan, inna after it would not have taken kasra, since it is the likely place for a single word. As for al-Kawāshī, he allowed kallā to be an alert, so that one pauses at what precedes it, and a rebuke, so that one pauses on it." As for Ibn Khālawayh, he patched together a strange and laughable patchwork. He said: "Kallā is begun with here because it has the sense of naʿam ḥaqqan (yes, truly), and it is not a rejection." This is speech with no comprehensible meaning. The truth is that kallā is a particle of rebuke and reproof, as Sībawayh said. Al-Zajjāj said: kallā is a rebuke and an alert, and that is your saying "kallā" to one who said to you something you reject, such as "So-and-so hates you" and the like, i.e. "desist from this and be alert to the error in it". Allah the Exalted said after His saying ﴿رَبِّي أَهانَنِ﴾: ﴿كَلَّا﴾, i.e. the matter is not so, because He may give abundance in this world to disbelievers whom He does not honour, and may restrict the prophets and the righteous for their improvement.
(أَنْ رَآهُ اسْتَغْنى): (أَنْ) is a particle forming a maṣdar and governing the accusative; with what it governs it is in the interpretation of a maṣdar, a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). (رَآهُ) is a past verb, its agent "he", and the hāʾ is the first direct object; the clause (اسْتَغْنى) is the second direct object. The hāʾ refers to man, and its meaning is "that he saw himself". The wording of Ibn Khālawayh is good. He said: If it is said to you, may you say "Zayd struck him" with the hāʾ referring to Zayd? Say: that is not permitted; the correct is "Zayd struck himself", because the agent in its entirety cannot be the object in its entirety. It is permitted in ﴿أَنْ رَآهُ﴾ only because it is among the verbs of doubt and knowledge, such as "ظَنَنْتُنِي" (I thought myself). If you make this word dual you say: "the two men certainly rebel, that they see themselves (rāʾāhumā) self-sufficient"; and "kallā, humans certainly rebel that they see themselves self-sufficient"; and you say to a woman when addressing her: "kallā, you certainly rebel that you saw yourself self-sufficient"; "kallā, you two certainly rebel that you saw yourselves self-sufficient"; "kallā, you women certainly rebel that you saw yourselves self-sufficient."
(إِنَّ إِلى رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعى): A resumptive passage, set out to address the rebellious man by way of iltifāt (shift). (إِنَّ) is a particle resembling the verb, (إِلى رَبِّكَ) is the fronted khabar of (إِنَّ), and (الرُّجْعى) is its postponed noun.
(أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يَنْهى عَبْداً إِذا صَلَّى): Muslim reported from Abū Hurayra that he said: Abū Jahl said: "Does Muhammad put his face in the dust among you?" It was said: "Yes." He said: "By al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā, if I see him do that I will tread on his neck and put his face in the dust." He said: So he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was praying, in order to tread on his neck. He said: Nothing took them by surprise except that he was retreating on his heels and shielding himself with his hands. It was said to him: "What is the matter with you?" He said: "Between me and him there is a trench of fire, a terror and wings." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Had he come near me, the angels would have snatched him limb by limb." (أَرَأَيْتَ): it was said before that when it has the sense of "tell me", as here, it governs two objects, the second of which is an interrogative clause; this has been mentioned more than once. Here it has been mentioned three times, and after the third an interrogative clause is stated explicitly, so it is in the position of its second object, and its first object is omitted, being a pronoun referring to (الَّذِي يَنْهى عَبْداً), which occurs as the first object of the first (أَرَأَيْتَ). As for the first (أَرَأَيْتَ), its first object is (الَّذِي) and its second object is omitted, being an interrogative clause like the clause occurring after the third (أَرَأَيْتَ). As for the second (أَرَأَيْتَ), no object is mentioned for it, neither first nor second: the first is omitted because the first object of the first (أَرَأَيْتَ) indicates it, and the second is omitted because the object of the third (أَرَأَيْتَ) indicates it. So the second has been omitted from the first, and the first from the third, and both from the second [Translator's note: the printed text reads "and the two from the third"; from the preceding explanation the second (أَرَأَيْتَ) seems to be meant]. This is not a case of tanāzuʿ (competition among verbs for one object), because tanāzuʿ requires a pronoun, and clauses are not replaced by pronouns; only single words are. Rather it is a case of omission by indication. The clause (يَنْهى) is a ṣila with no position; (عَبْداً) is the object of (يَنْهى); (إِذا) is an adverb of future time, of mere time, attached to (يَنْهى).
(أَرَأَيْتَ إِنْ كانَ عَلَى الْهُدى أَوْ أَمَرَ بِالتَّقْوى): (أَرَأَيْتَ): the hamza is for interrogation, (رَأَيْتَ) is a verb and agent, and its meaning is "tell me". (إِنْ) is conditional; (كانَ) is a defective past verb, in the position of jussive as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ), and the discussion of the response will follow. Its noun is latent, its implied form being "he"; (عَلَى الْهُدى) is its khabar. (أَوْ) is a conjunction; (أَمَرَ) is a past verb, its agent "he", conjoined to (كانَ عَلَى الْهُدى); (بِالتَّقْوى) is attached to (أَمَرَ).
(أَرَأَيْتَ إِنْ كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى أَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرى): (أَرَأَيْتَ): tell me. (إِنْ) is conditional; (كَذَّبَ) is a past verb in the position of jussive as the protasis, and (تَوَلَّى) is conjoined to (كَذَّبَ); the discussion of the response will follow also. The hamza is for interrogation, of confirmation and wonder; (لَمْ) is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; (يَعْلَمْ) is an imperfect verb jussive by (لَمْ); the bāʾ is a redundant preposition; (أَنَّ) with its noun, and the clause (يَرى) is its khabar; (أَنَّ) and what follows it stand in the place of the two objects of (يَعْلَمْ). As for the apodosis of the conditional that falls within the scope of the second and third, it is omitted, indicated by the interrogative clause, and the implied form is: "If he is on guidance or commands piety, did that forbidder not know that Allah sees?", and in the third: "If he denies and turns away, did he not know that Allah sees?", that is, on the assumption of the fāʾ. Al-Zamakhsharī took another course in parsing these verses, which we transmit to you so that we may then transmit Abū Ḥayyān's refutation, and you will see how the dispute rages over i'rab; in that is a polishing and clearing of the mind. The summary of al-Zamakhsharī's parsing: the object of the first (أَرَأَيْتَ) is the relative noun, and the second is redundant, repeated to emphasise the first; the second object of the first is the conditional clause that falls within the scope of the second, with its omitted apodosis, which is taken to be an interrogative clause, and it is the one stated explicitly within the scope of the third; the first object of the third is omitted, its implied form being "أَرَأَيْتَهُ", and the conditional clause after it and its apodosis, which is the interrogative clause stated explicitly, stand in the place of the second object. He said in establishing this parsing: "If you say: how is it correct that (أَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ) be an apodosis to the condition? I say: as it is correct in your saying 'If I honour you, will you honour me?' and 'If Zayd does good to you, will you do good to him?'" Abū Ḥayyān mocked this parsing and said: "What al-Zamakhsharī established here does not accord with what we established. Among that, he claimed that the conditional clause is in the position of the one object and the relative noun is the other. But with us the second object is only an interrogative clause, as in His saying: ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي تَوَلَّى وَأَعْطى قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدى أَعِنْدَهُ عِلْمُ الْغَيْبِ﴾, ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي كَفَرَ بِآياتِنا وَقالَ لَأُوتَيَنَّ مالًا وَوَلَداً أَطَّلَعَ الْغَيْبَ﴾, ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ ما تُمْنُونَ أَأَنْتُمْ تَخْلُقُونَهُ﴾, and this is frequent in the Qur'an. So the verse is to be analysed on that rule, and the object of the first (أَرَأَيْتَ) is made the relative noun, and after it comes (أَرَأَيْتَ), which demands two objects, and the second (أَرَأَيْتَ) likewise. The object of the second and third (أَرَأَيْتَ) is omitted, referring to (الَّذِي يَنْهى) in both, or to (عَبْداً) in the second and to (الَّذِي يَنْهى) in the third, according to the earlier disagreement on the return of the pronoun. Three demanders converge on the interrogative clause, so we say: the second object of (أَرَأَيْتَ), which is the interrogative clause, is omitted, indicated by the later interrogative; the object of the last (أَرَأَيْتَ) is omitted, indicated by the object of the first (أَرَأَيْتَ); and both are omitted together for the second (أَرَأَيْتَ), because the first indicates its object and the last indicates the other object of the third (أَرَأَيْتَ). These demanders are not by way of tanāzuʿ, because clauses cannot be replaced by pronouns; this is rather a case of omission other than tanāzuʿ. As for al-Zamakhsharī's allowing an interrogative clause to be the apodosis of a condition without the fāʾ, I do not know anyone who allowed it; rather they stated explicitly that the fāʾ is obligatory in everything that requires a request in any way, and it cannot be dropped except out of poetic necessity." As for Ibn Khālawayh, his parsing was extremely laughable, because he forgot or pretended to forget that there are omitted objects or an omitted apodosis, and contented himself with the apparent wording; how far this is from i'rab, especially in verses like these.
(كَلَّا لَئِنْ لَمْ يَنْتَهِ لَنَسْفَعاً بِالنَّاصِيَةِ ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ): (كَلَّا) is a rebuke and reproof of Abū Jahl. The lām is the preparatory lām for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa), because it enters a conditional particle to signal that the response after it is built on an oath before it, not on the condition; hence it is called the "informing" or "preparing" lām, because it prepares the response for the oath, that is, paves the way for it. (إِنْ) is conditional, (لَمْ) is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive, and (يَنْتَهِ) is an imperfect verb jussive by (لَمْ), its sign of jussive being the omission of the weak letter. (لَنَسْفَعاً): the lām is the response to the oath, in accordance with the established rule when oath and condition coincide; (نَسْفَعاً) is an imperfect verb indeclinable on fatḥa because of its attachment to the light nūn of emphasis, written with an alif in the codex according to the ruling of pause; the agent is latent, its implied form being "We". (بِالنَّاصِيَةِ) is attached to (نَسْفَعاً). (ناصِيَةٍ) is a badal from (النَّاصِيَةِ); substituting it for a definite noun is allowed though it is indefinite, because it is described; and the Basrans do not require agreement in the badal. It was read in the nominative on the implication "it is", and in the accusative as censure. (كاذِبَةٍ) and (خاطِئَةٍ) are two adjectives. The meaning of describing it as lying and sinning will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(فَلْيَدْعُ نادِيَهُ سَنَدْعُ الزَّبانِيَةَ كَلَّا لا تُطِعْهُ وَاسْجُدْ وَاقْتَرِبْ): The fāʾ is the "eloquent" fāʾ, i.e. "if he continues in his excess and persists in obstinacy and arrogance, then let him call." The lām is the lām of command, and (يَدْعُ) is an imperfect verb jussive by the lām of command, its sign of jussive being the omission of the wāw, its agent latent, its implied form being "he". The meaning of "calling the club" will come in the section on Rhetoric. The sīn is a particle of the future, and (نَدْعُ) is an imperfect nominative verb. The wāw has been dropped from the codex in every quiescent wāw followed by a quiescent lām. (الزَّبانِيَةَ) is the direct object. (كَلَّا) is an emphasis of the rebuke and reproof of Abū Jahl; (لا) is prohibitive, (تُطِعْهُ) is an imperfect verb jussive by (لا), the agent latent, its implied form being "you", and the hāʾ is the direct object. (اسْجُدْ) is an imperative verb, and (اقْتَرِبْ) is conjoined to (اسْجُدْ).

* Rhetoric:
1- In His saying: ﴿ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ﴾ there is a majāz ʿaqlī (rational figurative attribution): the forelock is described as lying and sinning, while in reality it is its owner. That is more eloquent than annexing it so as to say "the forelock of a liar, a sinner", because it is the thing spoken about.
2- In His saying ﴿فَلْيَدْعُ نادِيَهُ﴾ there is a majāz mursal (unrestricted figurative usage), the meaning being the people of the club: the club is not called; its people are called. So the place is mentioned and what is in it is meant, so it is a majāz mursal whose relation is locality. Al-nādī is the assembly in which people sit together, and the place is not called nādī until its people are in it. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "Nadā al-qawm nadwan (pattern ghazā): they gathered; from it is derived al-nādī, which is the assembly of the people for conversation." In al-Mukhtār: "Nādāhu: he sat with him in the nādī; tanādaw: they sat together in the nādī; al-nadiyy, on the pattern faʿīl, is the assembly of the people and their place of conversation, as are al-nadwa, al-nādī and al-muntadā; if the people disperse from it, it is not a nadiyy. From it Dār al-Nadwa, which Quṣayy built in Mecca, was named, because they used to nadaw in it, i.e. gather for consultation." When the Prophet ﷺ rebuked Abū Jahl, having forbidden him from praying, Abū Jahl said to him: "You know that there is no man in it, that is in Mecca, with a larger club than mine; I will fill this valley against you, if you wish, with swift horses and beardless men."

* Benefits:
1- The redundant bāʾ in the object of ʿalima: the redundancy of the bāʾ is regular in the object of ʿarafa (to know) and the like, and rare in the object of what governs two objects, but after ʿalima it is almost regular. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said:
وقد علم القبائل من معد ... إذا قبب بأبطحها بنينا
بأنّا المطعمون إذا قدرنا ... وأنّا المهلكون إذا ابتلينا
(The tribes of Maʿadd know, when we pitch tents in its valley, that we are the feeders when we are able, and the destroyers when we are tried.)
2- Do the badal and the mubdal minhu agree in definiteness and indefiniteness? Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Mufaṣṣal: "It is not a condition that the badal and the mubdal minhu agree in definiteness and indefiniteness; rather you may substitute either kind for the other. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّراطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ صِراطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾, and He said: ﴿بِالنَّاصِيَةِ ناصِيَةٍ كاذِبَةٍ خاطِئَةٍ﴾, except that it is not good to substitute an indefinite for a definite unless it is described, like nāṣiya." [Translator's note: the printed text reads «ناصبة», evidently a misprint for «ناصية».] As for the badal of an indefinite from an indefinite, an example is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿إِنَّ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ مَفازاً حَدائِقَ وَأَعْناباً﴾: His word (مَفازاً) is indefinite, and (حَدائِقَ) has been substituted for the indefinite. Similar is the poet's saying:
وكنت كذي رجلين رجل صحيحة ... ورجل رمى فيها الزمان فشلّت
(I was like one with two legs, one leg sound, and one leg in which time shot, and it withered.)
He substituted his saying "a sound leg" for "two legs", both being indefinite. An example of the badal of a definite from an indefinite is your saying "I passed by a man, Zayd". Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَإِنَّكَ لَتَهْدِي إِلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ صِراطِ اللَّهِ﴾: the second is definite by annexation, and He substituted it for the first, which is indefinite.
